ADDITIVE MANUFACTURING · POSTED SEP 23, 2026 · 5 MIN READ

A better print starts
before the slicer.

A successful print is rarely the result of one clever slicer setting. The bigger gains usually come from choosing the right process, designing for its constraints, and checking the part against its intended use.

Start with the job the part must do

Is the part a visual mock-up, a fixture, a replacement component, or a load-bearing assembly? The answer guides material, process, surface finish, dimensional expectations, and validation. Additive manufacturing builds a part layer by layer from digital model data, but different processes and materials produce different strengths and finishes.

Design around the process

Orientation changes support needs, surface quality, build time, and the direction in which layers are bonded. For fused-filament prints, strength is often direction-dependent, so place the part to keep the main load from pulling layers apart. For resin or powder processes, support strategy and evacuation of uncured material or loose powder also matter.

Check wall thickness, overhangs, bridges, holes, and long unsupported spans before slicing. Small holes and narrow gaps may print undersized or close up. When fit matters, make a small coupon or test feature first rather than assuming a nominal CAD dimension will produce a matching physical dimension.

Plan for assembly and post-processing

Clearance is a design choice. A press fit, sliding fit, and loose alignment fit need different allowances, and the right amount depends on the printer, material, orientation, and finishing steps. Include room for inserts, fasteners, sanding, coatings, or support removal where needed.

Use a repeatable print loop

  1. Confirm the material and machine suit the part’s purpose.
  2. Orient the part for load path, critical surfaces, and support access.
  3. Set process parameters from a known material profile, then change one variable at a time.
  4. Print a small fit or strength test if the design is new.
  5. Measure the finished part and record what should change next time.

Iteration is part of the process. A short test print can reveal whether the issue is geometry, orientation, material behavior, calibration, or post-processing before time is spent on a full build.
